# Umbraco Rules

Project conventions, enforced by code in `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco` where possible. The short version of the ten UmbraCommandments.

1. **Never put content behind a composition.** Removing a composition permanently deletes its content on every document that used it — no recovery through revisions. Compositions are for meta, settings, CTAs. Litmus test: *if we remove this composition later, is what remains still viable content?*
2. **There are six kinds of document type — file each in its folder.** Page (renders), Block (renders; lives in block list/grid; never used as a composition), Composition (composed onto others; never rendered, never pickable), Data (element; never renders — settings, events, people), Repository (container node; never renders), Repository Item (the pickable records inside a Repository).
3. **Data types never sit at the root of the data type tree.** Built-ins under `/Umbraco/<editor>`, custom ones under `/Custom/<editor>`. `DataTypeSavedHandler` enforces this on every save.
4. **Register in an `IComposer`, not Program.cs.** If `IUmbracoBuilder` can do it, it belongs in `Composers/`. Non-Umbraco concerns (CORS, App Insights) go in `WebApplicationBuilder` extension methods.
5. **Production runs in production mode.** Umbraco Application Url set, `--configuration Release`, HTTPS only, no model generation, no template editing. `appsettings.json` ships configured this way — don't soften it; put dev conveniences in `appsettings.Development.json`.
6. **Aliases are English and camelCase.** No exceptions.
7. **Dictionary keys are PascalCase with dots** (`My.Dictionary.Item`), and a dictionary folder never has values of its own.
8. **Media always lives in a folder.**
9. **The content root only holds Repositories.** The site hangs under the WWW `siteRoot` node; going multi-site means adding another Page beneath it, not re-architecting. Because WWW never renders, the site Page needs a **domain** or nothing answers on `/` — assign `/` for a single site, a hostname each for several.
10. **uSync everything — commit `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco/uSync/`.** Export is automatic; you should not need to trigger it. On Umbraco Cloud, use Umbraco Deploy instead.

Every team that has wired an AI assistant into their tools knows the pain. One connector for the ticket system, another for the file store, a third for the CMS, and each one is a custom adapter with its own auth, its own schema and its own bugs. Multiply the assistants by the tools and you get a tangle nobody wants to maintain.

The Model Context Protocol, or MCP, cuts through it. It is an open standard that describes how an assistant discovers what a tool can do and how it calls it. Build a server once and every MCP-aware client can use it.

The Model Context Protocol, or MCP, cuts through it. It is an open standard that describes how an assistant discovers what a tool can do and how it calls it. Build a server once and every MCP-aware client can use it.

A chatbot that only talks is a clever search box. The moment it can act, it becomes a colleague. MCP is what makes that jump practical, because it gives the assistant a standard way to see your systems and a standard way to change them.

Take a content management system. Without MCP, an assistant can suggest headlines. With MCP, it can look at your document types, create a page, fill in the fields, attach an image and publish it, all through the same tools a human editor would use.

The pieces are simple. A server advertises tools, each with a name, a description and a typed input schema. A client lists them, hands them to the model, and runs whichever one the model picks. Because the contract is machine-readable, the assistant can work out how to use a tool it has never seen before.

That also changes who can build integrations. Instead of waiting for a vendor to ship a plugin for your favourite assistant, you expose your own system as an MCP server in an afternoon and every compatible client can use it straight away.

That also changes who can build integrations. Instead of waiting for a vendor to ship a plugin for your favourite assistant, you expose your own system as an MCP server in an afternoon and every compatible client can use it straight away.

The best part is the feedback loop. Because the assistant can read as well as write, it can check its own work: create a document type, read it back, notice a missing template and fix it. Mistakes become visible and correctable instead of silently shipping.

Guardrails matter too. An MCP server decides which tools it exposes, so you can give an assistant exactly the access it needs and nothing more. Editors keep their confirmation prompts for anything destructive, and the humans stay in charge.

Every team that has wired an AI assistant into their tools knows the pain. One connector for the ticket system, another for the file store, a third for the CMS, and each one is a custom adapter with its own auth, its own schema and its own bugs. Multiply the assistants by the tools and you get a tangle nobody wants to maintain.

The Model Context Protocol, or MCP, cuts through it. It is an open standard that describes how an assistant discovers what a tool can do and how it calls it. Build a server once and every MCP-aware client can use it.

The pieces are simple. A server advertises tools, each with a name, a description and a typed input schema. A client lists them, hands them to the model, and runs whichever one the model picks. Because the contract is machine-readable, the assistant can work out how to use a tool it has never seen before.

That also changes who can build integrations. Instead of waiting for a vendor to ship a plugin for your favourite assistant, you expose your own system as an MCP server in an afternoon and every compatible client can use it straight away.

The blog is built and running. I fetched `/` and both posts with `curl -k`, and each returned 200. None of the pages contains "Could not render component".

## What I built
- **Block types:** Rich Text Block (`richTextBlock`), Image Block (`imageBlock`) and Callout Block (`calloutBlock`). They are in the Blocks folder.
- **Block grid:** the "Blog Body Block Grid" data type allows those three blocks. Umbraco filed it under `/Custom/Umbraco.BlockGrid`.
- **Page types:** `blogFrontPage` and `blogPost`, both in the Pages folder, each with a `blocks` property that uses the block grid. Each has its own template. `siteRoot` allows the front page, and the front page allows posts. I read each back after saving.
- **Media:** a "Blog" folder with four photos from `unsplash/`: network-lines-dots, code-on-screen, puzzle-hands and connected-structure.
- **Content under WWW:**
  - "Blog" (title "The MCP Blog") has a rich text block and a callout block.
  - The two posts are "Why MCP Is Awesome: One Protocol to Connect Them All" and "Why MCP Is Awesome: Real Work, Not Just Chat".
  - Each post has a title, date, excerpt, listing image and four body blocks: rich text, image, rich text, callout.
  - `get-page` shows all three pages as Published with their values, and the domain `/` is set on the front page.
- **Code:**
  - Templates `blogFrontPage.cshtml` and `blogPost.cshtml`, plus `Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml`.
  - Three adapters in `Views/Partials/blockgrid/Components/`, named after the block aliases and following the AGENTS.md example.
  - Three ViewComponents with views in `Views/Shared/Components/<Name>/Default.cshtml`.
  - Plain models in `Models/Blocks/`. I also added two `@using` lines to `_ViewImports.cshtml` and dropped its old `Umbraco.Cms.Web.Common.PublishedModels` using. `dotnet build` reports 0 warnings and 0 errors, and `npm run build` finished.

## How to view it
Umbraco is running in the background, started with `dotnet run` from `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco`.
- **Front page:** https://localhost:44317/
- **Posts:** `/why-mcp-is-awesome-one-protocol-to-connect-them-all/` and `/why-mcp-is-awesome-real-work-not-just-chat/`
- **Backoffice:** https://localhost:44317/umbraco, logging in as admin@example.com / 1234567890.

## What I checked on the rendered pages
- Home has 1 rich text block, 1 callout and 2 post cards linking to the posts. Each post has 2 rich text blocks, 1 image block and 1 callout.
- The four image URLs and `site.css` all return 200, and the page titles and body text appear.

## Issues and caveats
- My first start returned 500. I had written `Layout = "_Layout.cshtml"`, which Razor looked for in `/Views/` instead of `Views/Shared`. I changed it to `"_Layout"`, rebuilt and restarted, and it then returned 200.
- I haven't looked at the pages in a browser, so the Tailwind styling is unchecked. I only confirmed the CSS file loads.
- The Umbraco process is still running, so stop it before your next `dotnet build`.
